hook: Propane tanks at a barbecue hold liquid propane at about 9 atm. At that pressure the ideal gas law badly mispredicts how much fuel is inside, because propane molecules are so close together that they pull on each other and finally condense. Real gases follow PV = nRT only when their molecules are far apart and fast.

figure.caption: Attractions lower the pressure below ideal; particle volume raises the volume above ideal.

chain.effect: a particle near the wall is pulled back, so the measured pressure is lower than ideal

chain.cause: Attractions matter more when particles are close and slow
chain.effect: deviations grow at high pressure and low temperature
at very high pressure the real volume is larger than ideal

chain.cause: High temperature and low pressure make both effects small
chain.effect: real gases behave most ideally there, especially small, weakly attracting ones like He

ideas: Ideal gas: PV/nRT = 1. Below 1, attractions dominate; above 1, particle volume dominates.
Attractions lower the pressure: worst for polar or polarizable molecules, at low T and high P.
Particle volume raises the volume: worst at very high P and for large molecules.
Most ideal: high temperature, low pressure, small particles with weak attractions.

misconception.wrong: A real gas deviates from ideal behavior only because its molecules take up space.
misconception.right: At ordinary high pressures the bigger effect is usually attraction, which makes the pressure lower than ideal. Particle volume only takes over at very high pressure.

summary: Real gases depart from PV = nRT because their particles attract each other, which lowers the pressure, and take up space, which raises the volume at very high pressure. Deviations are largest at high pressure and low temperature and for particles with strong intermolecular forces; gases are most ideal at high temperature and low pressure.
